en: Same material, same pawns, same rook in both chapters — the ONLY difference is one square of the white king. On e3 it commits to the game and the position is won. On e2 it stays sheltered and the very same game is only a draw.
A king marching toward the action
The same king, one square back: only a draw

Nothing forces this move yet — but instead of retreating to safety, White's king advances toward the theatre of operations, ready to support the e-pawn AND to threaten the g6-pawn. This activity, and nothing else, is what will decide the whole ending.

Just one square less, and yet everything flips: the king stays sheltered on the 2nd rank instead of committing. No White move from here ever recreates a winning chance again — the tablebase is categorical: this king, left passive, only draws now.
Black's rook looks for activity of its own, aiming at the g3-pawn.

The king keeps marching: it defends g3 along the way, and edges even closer to the g6-pawn, which becomes a genuine target. Compare with the other chapter — the same king, left on the 2nd rank, could never do this.
Black's king doesn't even need to defend actively any more: it calmly recentralises, certain that White's passivity will never cause trouble again.

This is DOMINATION: one single queen square that attacks the knight AND simultaneously covers its only two flight squares. The knight is lost before the queen even takes it — that is the entire difference from a plain attack.
One square governs the knight's entire fate
Attacking without dominating: the knight escapes

THE domination square: the queen checks along the 8th rank, AND covers b6 and c7 on the a5-d8 diagonal — the ONLY two squares the a8-knight could ever flee to. One square, three jobs at once: that is what "domination" means.

The queen does attack the knight, straight down the a-file — but it covers NEITHER b6 NOR c7. The win is still there (the queen always beats a lone knight eventually), but this is no longer domination: just an attack, and attacks can be dodged.
Black's king steps aside — it has no other choice, and it changes nothing at all: the knight remains doomed no matter where the king goes.

The knight simply had nowhere to go — neither b6 nor c7 had been free since move one. This is what separates domination from a plain attack: the piece was already lost BEFORE the queen came to collect it.
The knight escapes — and even finds time to give a check on its way out. Compare with Qd8+: the entire difference between the two chapters comes down to a single queen square.
White's king steps to safety; the game is still won, but the hunt must now start over — the very job Qd8+ had finished in a single move.

Black has nothing left but a king and a rook against a king and a queen: objectively, this has been lost for a long time, nothing can change that verdict. But STALEMATE is a practical resource — the last card for a side that has no other left.
The only hope: force the blunder
The correct defence: refuse the gift

Objectively the game has been lost for a long time — queen versus rook, no move will ever change that verdict. But the rook attacks the queen, and hands White a question that must be answered precisely.

The queen gobbles the rook — the most natural reflex in the world, materially free. And yet: the queen locks down the entire 7th rank (g7 AND h7 in one move), White's king holds g8, and Black's king is NOT in check. STALEMATE. The whole lesson lives in this one square: a position lost for hours that turns back into a draw because the last black piece fell with no check and no room to breathe.
The only thing White must do: NOT recapture the rook from that particular square. Any square that keeps the queen active off the 7th rank wins normally — the trap only exists for whoever rushes in.
The rook keeps harassing — it's all the losing side has left. None of these checks lead anywhere: White's king has all the room in the world to step aside.
And the conversion carries on, exactly as if Black's rook had never tried anything at all.

This is THE principle of two weaknesses, Capablanca's rule: an isolated passed pawn on the queenside occupies Black's king all by itself — it would hold forever if that were the only issue. But the kingside is a SECOND weakness, and one king cannot guard two at once.
Two weaknesses, one king
Guard the other weakness instead? The other one falls
White doesn't rush toward the a-pawn or the kingside: the king waits to see where Black's king commits before choosing its own side.
Black's king rushes toward the only pawn it can still stop — the FIRST weakness already occupies its entire king, on its own.
This time Black's king picks the OTHER weakness: it stays to guard its f-pawn, leaving the a-pawn to fend for itself.

While Black's king is busy at the other end of the board, the f-pawn advances with no black piece able to oppose it. The SECOND weakness takes shape — and it, not the a-pawn, is what will decide the game.
Nothing else to do: Black's king must continue its journey toward a5.
White's king reaches ITS weakness too — while Black went to fetch theirs at the far end of the board.
The pawn falls — but it's a fool's bargain: in grabbing it, Black's king has banished itself four files from everything else.

THE point of the lesson: White's king captures in turn, and the surviving f-pawn has no one left to stop it — Black's king is far too distant. One king can never guard two weaknesses at once: exactly Capablanca's rule.
With no one to bother it, the a-pawn charges alone toward promotion.
Black's king finally rushes toward it — but each side can only be in one place at a time, and it starts two moves too late.
Too late regardless: only one square remains before the queen.
The queen is born in peace. Two weaknesses, one king: whichever one it chooses to guard, it is always the OTHER one that decides the game.

A perfectly symmetric position, and yet nobody wants to move: having the move is a curse — the SAME position with the other side to move would sink the other camp instead. The trebuchet is zugzwang in its purest form.
Whoever moves loses
The other defence, same verdict

White has the move — and that alone is lost. The e4 pawn cannot advance (blocked), the only thing to play is the king, and EVERY king move gives up either the guard on his own pawn or the watch on Black's. Kc6 lets go of e4.
The other way to yield: the white king steps aside on the other wing. The result is identical — NO square keeps everything at once.
The pawn falls, and Black's pawn has nobody left in front of it. The game is decided: a free pawn, a king escorting it, the other king too far to get back.
The white king tries to come back — too late, he is short of tempi he no longer has.
A queen appears at the far end of the board, never once threatened. Sealed on the very first move — a move that was not even bad, except for existing.
Same road, same ending. The trebuchet has exactly one variable — whose move it is — and it alone decides everything.

Two blocked pawns against one, a position that looks won — and yet pushing right away is only a draw. Triangulation is the art of losing a tempo through a three-square detour, landing back on the same position with the opponent to move. A round trip that changes everything.
The triangle that hands over the move
The other defence: mate in two
The hasty push only draws
Neither a check nor a push: the king sets off on a detour. Patience — that is the whole chapter.

The reflex: “I have two pawns against one, I push.” And half the point evaporates: the black king dashes to c8, takes the pawn that sacrifices itself, and reaches the other one in time. Triangulation wasn't a nicety — it was the ONLY method.
The black king keeps his one job: watching the breakthrough squares c6/d6.
Second corner of the triangle. The white king has THREE squares (d5-e5-d4) for this dance; the black king has only two (c6-d7) — that asymmetry decides everything.

Back to the start — compare with the very first diagram: the pieces are EXACTLY the same. Only the move has changed hands. The white king gained no square; he gained a tempo, which amounts to the same thing.
The black king must give way — he has no waiting move left, unlike the white king three moves earlier.
And the breakthrough begins, carried by the tempo won inside the triangle.
The pawn finally advances, ESCORTED. The course used to stop here — too early: “the conversion is mechanical” is easy to write, and the student never saw it. Here it is, all the way to mate.
The capture is all but forced: on 16…Kb8, 17.c7+ Ka8 18.c8=Q is mate at once (see the next chapter).
Black's king declines the capture — and it is worse. The c-pawn is now backed by its neighbour, and c7 comes with check.
And not 17.bxc6, which leads nowhere: Black's c6 pawn is irrelevant, only the b-pawn matters. White's king steps up to escort it.
The black pawn runs — three squares behind, it will never arrive.
Queening with check, which rules out any resistance.
Mate. That is what the triangle Kd5-Ke5-Kd4 was worth: one tempo, and that tempo was worth the whole game.
Check, and the king has only the corner.
Mate. Two connected pawns escorted by their king against a cornered king: there never was a defence, only two ways to lose.
The only defence — and it is more than enough: bxc6+ and the black king mops up what's left.

Troitsky, 1906: the black king is shut in a three-square box — h1, h2, h3 — by a king and one pawn. While the door stays locked, the white knight goes on its rounds, eats the pawns one by one… then sacrifices itself to set its own pawn free. High art, wound like clockwork.
The knight's rounds
If Black pushes h5
The greedy capture
The other capture

The ONLY winning move — the opposite of the two natural captures, which merely draw (see the traps). The point: Kf2 and the g3-pawn lock the h1-h2-h3 cage; the knight attacks h4 with all eternity ahead of it.
Grabbing the central pawn, defended by nobody — pure reflex. But that pawn hung for a reason:
Same family of error, different culprit: the pawn abandons g3 — the lock of the cage.
The black king can only shuttle. Note that …g4-g3 does not exist: the white pawn owns that square.
The other serious defence: pulling the h6-pawn out of the knight's rounds. But the knight's wheel has more than one spoke:
First errand: the h4-pawn.
The knight sets off again via f5 — bound for h6. The cage, meanwhile, does not budge an inch.
Second errand. Black is down to the g4-pawn — precisely the one blockading White's own.
The loop tightens: d4 prepares the hop into f3.
The study's point: the knight offers itself to the g4-pawn. Taking frees g3; declining lets knight and king pick up g4 next move — the tablebase gives Black nothing better than to accept.
The rounds are done: all three black pawns gone, the g3-pawn passed, and the black king never left its box.
The black king finally gets out — to chase a train that has already left.
g8=Q next. From move one the whole study fitted in a sentence: the cage cost only TWO warders, so the knight was free — free even to die at the right moment.
Captured — and the carousel restarts, one square along.
Back through the starting square: the g2-f4 circuit aims at h5 exactly as it aimed at h4.
Second pawn. The third still waits on g4, nailed to the spot.
Third pawn — with check this time: no sacrifice needed, the h5 version collapses even faster.
Knight and pawn against a bare king: g4-g5-g6… The moral is the same in every branch: the black pawns were never a force, only a pantry.
…the black king takes it back and walks out of the cage through the same door.

The tally: not one white pawn left, a black pawn still on h6 — WHITE is the one who must hold the draw (his king reaches the corner: rook pawn, the known fortress). From winner to defender in two moves.
The knight scoops up g4 in passing, but:
…everything evaporates: king against king and h-pawn — the white king runs to h1, draw. Both captures reach the same dead end; only the locked cage of 1.Ng2! kept the loot intact.

Two lone knights against a bare king can never force mate — stalemate always looms. But if the weaker side still has a pawn, it can supply the one spare move that avoids stalemate at just the right moment, and mate becomes possible again.
Blockade the pawn, tighten the net
The king advances too soon

One knight goes to blockade the pawn on h3 — it must never advance again, or Black's king loses its only spare move. The other knight and White's king then close in on Black's king, never once offering stalemate.
Seems logical — bring White's king into the fight without delay. But no knight has gone to blockade the pawn yet, and without that blockade the whole plan collapses.
White's king closes in too — the blockading knight stays put, motionless, while the rest of the setup tightens.
The net closes: Black's king has only h1 left, and the pawn has nowhere to go.
Forced — and it's exactly this spare move, kept in reserve from the start, that finally allows mate: without it, this would be stalemate.
Mate. Verified from the root: seventeen moves to mate, and not a single stalemate along the way.
Black's king escapes toward the pawn, which stays free to advance or be traded off as the defence needs — the blockading square was never taken, and the draw holds.

Rook's pawn on the sixth, enemy rook IN FRONT of its own pawn: the position every tournament player ends up defending. Vančura showed in 1924 where the rook holds the draw — from the side, never from behind. Counter-intuitive, and eternal.
The rook on the flank
The king stays across
The poisoned pawn
The king who deserts his post
The white king comes to shepherd the pawn and free his rook — the ONLY winning plan. Watch the f6-rook greet him.
The other try: evict the black king first.
The SIDEWAYS check, Vančura's trademark: the rook strikes from the rank where it ALSO hits the pawn. The white king has no shelter on those ranks.

“My king will help”… and everything collapses: a7! races through at once — the black king has stepped into his own rook's path, leaving it neither useful checks nor a safe rank. Vančura's king NEVER leaves g6-g7.
And back to the pawn's rank. This carousel can spin for a thousand years.
The pawn finally drops?… and the a8-rook recaptures on the square: Rxa6, and you are inside “The Rook Mate” — on the wrong end. The flank rook was meant to PIN the pawn down, never to eat it.
Above all, don't take a6 — see the poisoned-pawn chapter.
The white king fled the checks toward the centre? The rook keeps ITS rank and keeps hitting the pawn: while it hangs, the a8-rook stands sentry and the pawn is nailed down.
The b6-f6 pendulum: always the sixth, always the pawn at gunpoint. Nothing progresses, nothing ever will — Vančura's draw.
One square is enough — but not any square: the black king stays OPPOSITE the pawn, out of his own rook's line. f7 or g8 would be outrun.
Back to sentry duty — else the pawn dropped.
And the black king resumes his post. Two squares for half a point: g7 and g6.
The pawn asked for nothing more: on the 7th it changes the geometry — the flank rook no longer reaches it, the a8-rook is free.
The rook isn't defending the pawn — it is banishing the enemy king from half the board. Cut off by two files, that king never rejoins the game: the pawn can walk home alone.
A banished king no longer exists
The rook already owns the f-file: two whole files (f, plus g-h behind the black king) he can never set foot on. So the pawn advances ALONE — no need to wait for the white king.
The black king edges closer… to nothing at all. The cut-off isn't about distance but about a WALL: two rook-files, impassable.
The black king finally reaches the wall — far too late, and unable to cross it regardless.
The rook gives up the f-file — no longer needed, the pawn is one step from queening and the black king, banished since move one, still can't do a thing about it.
The rook closes the net — not a square left for the black king.
Mate. The black king never took part in the game after move one: that is the entire meaning of a two-file cut-off.

Dark-squared bishop, a-pawn: the "wrong bishop" — and yet White wins. Because the famous fortress has an entry requirement: the defending king must REACH the a8 corner. It stands three steps away; the game is therefore a race, and it is won with a two-square wall: the bishop bars b8, the king bars b7. Exactly one bishop move builds that wall in time.
Bf4! — the wall before the push
The hasty push — and the fortress snaps shut

The move of the ending. Of the six legal bishop moves, ONLY this one wins (verified: the other five draw) — f4 is the one square that reaches the b8-h2 diagonal in a SINGLE tempo, the diagonal that locks the b8 door. The pawn can wait: barrier first.
